name: Garamantes
info: The Garamantes were an ancient people of the Fezzan in southern Libya who, from at least 1000 BC to the late 7th century AD, built a desert kingdom on qanat irrigation and trans-Saharan trade.

facts.homeland: The Fezzan region of southern Libya, centred on the Wadi al-Ajjal; their capital Garama lay at modern Germa, about 150 km west of Sabha, with an earlier capital at Zinkekara; other sites include Fewet, Saniat bin Huwaydi, and the southern oases of Ghat and Barkat
facts.period: Settlement in the Fezzan at least as early as 1000 BC; a powerful polity from the 6th century BC; foggara irrigation appearing between 200 BC and 200 CE; a major regional power from the mid-2nd century AD; the end of the kingdom in the late 7th century AD
facts.known: foggara (qanat) irrigation tapping fossil water; the first urban society in a major desert not centred on a river; control of trade routes between the Niger Bend, Lake Chad and the Mediterranean; slave raiding and trading; inscriptions in a Libyan script that are only partly decipherable; conflict with Rome
facts.sources: Greco-Roman writers from Herodotus in the 5th century BC to Strabo, Tacitus, Pliny the Elder, Ptolemy and Solinus; excavations at Germa in the 1960s; satellite imagery published in 2011; skeletal and isotopic studies by Sergi (1951), Chamla (1968), Mattingly et al. (2003), Lahr et al. (2010), Nikita et al. (2011), Ricci et al. (2013) and Power et al. (2019)

t: The Garamantes mined fossil water from under the desert through a network of tunnels and shafts, the foggaras, which supported farming and a large population in the Fezzan.
Their largest town, Garama, had about four thousand inhabitants, with another six thousand in villages within a 5 km radius, and up to 50,000 people may have lived in the whole wadi.
The fall of the ground water level over the centuries of the kingdom may have contributed to its end in the late 7th century AD.
dyk: The Roman traveller Julius Maternus journeyed with the king of the Garamantes for about four months from Garama to a land called Agisymba, whose people the king presented as his subjects.
ev: Peoples who may have descended from Berber and Toubou tribes and Saharan pastoralists are settled in the Fezzan
The Garamantes form a powerful polity controlling trade routes between the Niger Bend and the Mediterranean
Herodotus describes the Garamantes as a very great nation who herded cattle and farmed dates
Lucius Cornelius Balbus and other Romans capture fifteen Garamantian settlements in response to continuous raiding
Septimius Severus captures the capital city of Garama
The Garamantian kingdom comes to an end as the ground water level falls

sections.origins:
The Garamantes may have descended from Libyco-Berber tribes, Toubou tribes and Saharan pastoralists who settled in an area of the Fezzan region, in present-day southern Libya, at least as early as 1000 BC. At the Takarkori rockshelter, Final Pastoral peoples restructured their society around 3000 BP and created burial sites for several hundred individuals, with non-local luxury goods and drum-type architecture; this made way for the development of the Garamantian kingdom. People of the Tichitt culture in southeastern Mauritania may also have contributed to Garamantian domestic architecture and ceramics, possibly through the presence of Sahelian women married into Garamantian society.

From the 6th century BC the Garamantes formed a powerful polity, and they emerged as a major regional power in the mid-2nd century AD, with a kingdom of roughly 180,000 km2. What language they spoke is open to conjecture. The linguist Roger Blench has noted that they wrote in a Libyan script although there is no evidence they spoke Berber, and has suggested that a Nilo-Saharan language related to Songhay or to Teda is the most likely hypothesis.
sections.society:
The Garamantes developed the first urban society in a major desert that was not centred on a river system. Excavations in the 1960s uncovered part of their capital, Garama, at modern Germa; an earlier capital, Zinkekara, lay nearby. Research indicates about eight major towns, three of which had been examined by 2004, and many smaller settlements. Garama had a population of around four thousand, with another six thousand living in villages within a 5 km radius, and up to 50,000 people could have lived in the whole wadi.

This life rested on the foggaras, a network of tunnels and shafts that mined fossil water from under the limestone layer beneath the desert sand. Their dating is disputed: they appear between 200 BC and 200 CE and remained in use until at least the 7th century. The system supported a strong agricultural economy and was maintained with slave labour. Skeletal studies by Nikita and colleagues (2011) found little sign of regular warfare or strenuous activity, and low sexual dimorphism in the upper limbs consistent with an agricultural population.
sections.beliefs:
Little is known of the beliefs of the Garamantes. What survives comes mainly from their dead: the archaeological remains of the kingdom include numerous tombs and cemeteries, and Mattingly and colleagues (2003) note that some light-skinned Libyans were buried in monumental graves. Roman writers describe the Garamantes as bearing ritual scars and tattoos.

Burial seems to have drawn people of different origins into one custom. The remains of a young woman from sub-Saharan Africa, dated to the 1st millennium BC and wearing a lip plug of a kind associated with Sahelian groups, were found among other sub-Saharan Africans in a Garamantian cemetery. Power and colleagues (2019) argue that the ornament shows that some Garamantes shared material culture with Sahelian societies, while the burial itself shows that such people were integrated into the normal funerary rituals of Garamantian society. Inscriptions were also placed in the tombs of Garamantian cemeteries, such as those of Saniat bin Huwaydi, though most of them cannot be read.
sections.arts:
The Garamantes left numerous tombs, forts and cemeteries, and satellite imagery published in 2011 revealed more of the buildings and structures they constructed. Their greatest work of engineering was the foggara system, which brought water from under the desert to their fields, and its builders have been described as brilliant farmers, resourceful engineers and enterprising merchants.

They had a script of their own. Sites near Jarma, the Garamantian capital, have abundant inscriptions cut or painted on dark grey amphorae and in tombs, and a project under the British Library has digitised most of them. They may have used a nearly indecipherable form of proto-Tifinagh: the inscriptions are in Berber characters, but only some can be read. Blench (2019) lists the explanations scholars have offered: the messages may have been deliberately coded for particular readers, may have been playful, or may have been written in a non-Berber language, perhaps Nilo-Saharan or something unknown. Rock art across the Sahara as far as southern Mauritania, some showing a war chariot chasing a man, is likely testimony to Garamantian mobility.
sections.exchange:
The king of the Garamantes controlled trade routes that reached deep into sub-Saharan Africa, to the regions between the Niger Bend and Lake Chad; the southern oases of Ghat and Barkat were bases for traders travelling into tropical Africa. Part of this trade was in people. Herodotus wrote that they used four-horse chariots to hunt the "Troglodyte Ethiopians", though Sonja and Carlos Magnavita (2018) treat this as possibly a speculative tale. In the last millennium BCE, agropastoralists at Dhar Tichitt in Mauritania were repeatedly raided from the north by people archaeologists think were Libyco-Berbers or Garamantes, perhaps taken as labourers to the Fezzan. Ostraca from the Roman fort of Bu Djem document Garamantian traders and black slaves.

Relations with Rome were often hostile. Tacitus wrote that the Garamantes assisted the rebel Tacfarinas and raided Roman coastal settlements. According to Pliny the Elder, Lucius Cornelius Balbus and other Romans captured fifteen of their settlements in 19 BC, and in 202 AD Septimius Severus captured Garama. The traveller Julius Maternus also accompanied a Garamantian king on an expedition of about four months to Agisymba.
sections.legacy:
The decline of the Garamantes may have been connected to worsening climatic conditions or to the overuse of water. Their irrigation drew on fossil water, a non-renewable resource, and over the centuries of the kingdom the ground water level fell, contributing to its end in the late 7th century AD. Land that is now Saharan desert was once farmland of fairly good quality, improved by Garamantian irrigation.

The Garamantes have become a subject of debate about who they were. Roman writers saw some as very dark-skinned and others as close to the Berber peoples, and Mattingly and colleagues (2003) concluded that this mixed picture most likely reflects the ancient reality. Later skeletal studies disagree in detail: Lahr and colleagues (2010) found that Roman-era skeletons from the Fezzan clustered most closely with Neolithic Sahelian samples, while Nikita and colleagues (2011) found the Garamantes an isolated population. Ricci and colleagues (2013) found gene flow, probably from sub-Saharan populations and more evident in women. The practice of stealing women from the south was attributed to the Garamantes and to later peoples such as the Tuareg and Tebu.

summary: The Garamantes were a people of the Fezzan in southern Libya who, from at least 1000 BC until the late 7th century AD, built towns in the desert on water drawn from deep underground. They controlled trade routes across the Sahara, including a trade in enslaved people, fought with Rome, and wrote in a script that is still only partly understood.
references: Eamonn Gearon, The Sahara: A Cultural History (Signal Books, 2011)
notes: The article's reference list holds only works on the concept of race (Pearson, Templeton, Wagner et al., etc.), none about the Garamantes, so references are left empty; in-text citations (Mattingly et al. 2003, Fentress 2011, Blench 2006, 2019) are not given in full.
The quotation 'brilliant farmers, resourceful engineers, and enterprising merchants' is unattributed in the article, so it is given without a name.
Beliefs section is thin: the article has no section on religion; I kept to burials, ritual scars and tomb inscriptions.
The article calls the 6th-century BC polity 'in northern Libya', which conflicts with the Fezzan being southern Libya; I left out 'northern'.
Start -1000 ("at least as early as 1000 BC") and end 700 ("late 7th century AD") are approximations.
The article's racial terminology (quoted from older studies) was paraphrased neutrally.
